key_terms.meaning: Machine driven by the engine or APU that converts mechanical power into electrical power at a controlled voltage and frequency
A thick copper bar that collects generator output and feeds it to many load circuits through individual protection
Relay circuits that trip the generator contactor when output leaves its allowed band, so bad power never reaches the bus
Transformer plus rectifier that steps 115 V AC down and converts it to 28 V DC
Device that converts DC into AC at the frequency the load needs, e.g. 28 V DC to 115 V AC 400 Hz
Single-winding transformer with a tapped winding that raises or lowers AC voltage with little loss
Alkaline cell, about 1.2 V per cell, with low internal resistance and high discharge current, standard for engine starting and emergency DC
Small air-driven turbine that drops into the slipstream and spins a generator when all main power is lost
Generator with a fixed magnet rotor; needs no field supply, so it survives loss of all DC and feeds essential AC
Extended-range twin-engine operations: rules that fix how far a twin may fly from an alternate airport, sized by emergency power and time available
Exterior red (left), green (right) and white (tail) lights that show the aircraft's heading to other traffic at night
Standard case size, connector layout and mounting for avionics boxes, so boxes from different makers interchange
Electromagnetic interference is unwanted coupling into a circuit; electromagnetic compatibility is the ability to work beside other equipment without either disturbing the other
Instrument that reads the difference between total pressure and static pressure, and displays it as speed
Instrument that reads static pressure alone and displays height above a set pressure datum
Temperature of the gas leaving the engine, measured by thermocouples; a direct check on turbine health and thrust
Voltage regulator that varies field current by squeezing a stack of carbon discs, whose resistance falls as pressure rises
Slow-blow fuse-like device that carries normal current indefinitely but opens on a heavy sustained fault
Bus arrangement where generators run in parallel on the ground or when needed, but feed separate halves in flight so one fault stays local
AC whose frequency follows engine speed instead of being fixed at 400 Hz; loads must accept the wider band
Tank probes plus a computer that convert capacitance or resistance changes into fuel mass or volume in the cockpit

takeaways: A generator is only useful once its voltage is regulated, its output is switched to a busbar, and its faults are cleared before wiring overheats.
Converters exist because different loads need different forms of power: 115 V AC 400 Hz, 28 V DC, and on newer aircraft 235 V AC variable frequency and 270 V DC.
The battery starts the engine or APU and bridges the gap between losing all generators and getting another source online.
The ram air turbine and the permanent magnet generator are the last line of defence, and ETOPS rules decide how much time that line must buy.
Aircraft lights divide by user (crew, cabin, outside world), and each group gets its own supply, control and failure requirement.
An avionics box must be packaged to a standard form, cooled by a defined path, and designed to meet interference limits, or it will not be fitted to an aircraft.
The airspeed indicator reads total minus static pressure; the altimeter reads static pressure alone.
Voltage regulators all do one thing: compare output with a reference and move field current to close the gap.
Protection is chosen from the derated rating of the wire, not from the load current, otherwise the wire becomes the fuse.
Bus architecture decides how much aircraft is lost when one generator or one bus fails.
bank_note: Long answers here are marked on the chain from source to load: generation, regulation, conversion, distribution, protection, and the failure case that each architecture is designed to survive.

bank.q: Explain how a generator's output reaches an aircraft load. Cover the busbar, the generator contactor, and over-voltage and under-voltage protection.
outline: Generator output rectified or regulated to the bus voltage
Generator contactor connects output to the busbar only when voltage and frequency are inside limits
Over-voltage trip opens the contactor before loads are damaged
Under-voltage trip prevents a failed generator from dragging the bus down
Busbar feeds each load through its own fuse or circuit breaker

bank.q: Compare lead-acid and nickel-cadmium aircraft batteries: construction, cell voltage, charge and discharge behaviour, and where each is used.
outline: Lead-acid: about 2 V per cell, lead and lead-dioxide plates, dilute sulphuric acid
NiCd: about 1.2 V per cell, nickel hydroxide and cadmium plates, alkaline electrolyte
NiCd has lower internal resistance, so higher cranking current
Lead-acid is cheaper and simpler but heavier for the same capacity
NiCd tolerates deep discharge better; both need venting and temperature control

bank.q: Describe the internal and external lighting of a transport aircraft. State the supply and control for each group.
outline: Exterior: navigation red/green/white, anti-collision beacons, strobes, landing and taxi lights
Flight compartment: panel flood, integral post lights, map light, dimming control
Cabin: ceiling and sidewall lighting, emergency floor-path lighting on its own battery supply
Emergency exit signs and floor path lights must survive loss of main power
Dimming by variable resistance or pulse-width control

bank.q: Explain the construction and working of a vibrating-contact voltage regulator, and state its main drawbacks.
outline: Electromagnet coil across the generator output pulls an armature
Armature carries a contact that opens and closes the field circuit
Field current is chopped; average field current falls as voltage rises
Spring tension sets the regulated voltage
Drawbacks: contact wear, radio interference from arcing, coarse regulation

bank.q: Explain the pitot-static system and how the airspeed indicator and the altimeter use it.
outline: Pitot tube faces the airflow and senses total pressure
Static ports on the fuselage side sense static pressure
Airspeed indicator capsule sees total pressure inside and static outside; deflection gives dynamic pressure
Airspeed is computed from dynamic pressure and air density
Altimeter is an evacuated capsule seeing static pressure only; a stack and linkage convert pressure to height
Blocked pitot or static ports give specific false readings

bank.q: An aircraft has a 28 V DC system with a 100 A generator. Explain how a TRU and an inverter are used to feed a 115 V AC 400 Hz load and a 28 V DC load, and why both converters are needed.
outline: TRU: transformer steps AC down, rectifier gives DC; used where main supply is AC
Inverter: DC to AC at fixed frequency for AC instruments
Loads dictate the conversion, not the source
Conversion losses and heat must be allowed for
In modern architecture many small converters replace one large unit

bank.q: A 28 V DC feeder carries 40 A continuously and passes through a zone where the ambient temperature derates the wire to 70 percent of its rated current. Explain how you would choose the protection device.
outline: Find the wire's rated current from the table for that gauge
Apply temperature and bundle derating factors
Protection device rating must be at or below the derated wire rating, not the 40 A load
Check the time-current curve: fault current must clear before wire damage
Check voltage drop over the run and short-circuit withstand

bank.q: Describe how the ram air turbine is deployed and what it feeds, and explain how ETOPS rules use the available emergency power time.
outline: Deployment on loss of AC bus or by pilot action; automatic on some types
Governed to constant frequency, usually 115 V AC 400 Hz
Feeds essential AC and, through a TRU, essential DC
Load shedding leaves only flight controls, essential instruments, one radio
ETOPS diversion time is set by the certified time with this power available
Pilot must descend to a lower altitude where the RAT is effective

bank.q: Explain how a tachometer and an EGT indicator turn engine speed and temperature into cockpit readings.
outline: Tachometer: small generator or magnetic pick-up gives a voltage or pulse rate proportional to shaft speed
Indicator is a voltmeter calibrated in percent RPM
EGT: thermocouples in the exhaust stream generate a small millivolt signal
Cold junction compensation and amplification in the indicator
Indicator scale in degrees Celsius; limits marked in red

bank.q: Describe the packaging, cooling and EMI requirements for a line-replaceable avionics unit, and name the standards used.
outline: ARINC 600 or ARINC 404 case, front-loading, standard connectors
DOD / MIL standards for shock, vibration, humidity and altitude
Cooling by forced air through the case, or conduction to a cold plate
Heat load must be removed within the bay's cooling budget
EMI: shielding, filtering, grounding, bonding; emission and susceptibility limits
Lightning and HIRF protection as separate requirements

bank.q: Compare the A320 and B787 electrical architectures and evaluate why the B787 moved to 235 V AC variable frequency and 270 V DC.
outline: A320: 115 V AC 400 Hz from IDGs, 28 V DC from TRUs, batteries for emergency
B787: 235 V AC variable frequency from large starter-generators, 270 V DC from TRUs
Higher voltage means lower current for the same power, so lighter cables
Variable frequency removes the constant-speed drive, saving weight and maintenance
Trade-off: new protection devices, arc-fault detection, higher insulation demands

bank.q: Explain split, parallel and split-parallel bus systems. Analyse what happens to the aircraft in each when one generator fails in flight.
outline: Split: each generator feeds its own bus; a fault is confined to one side
Parallel: generators share the bus; load sharing needs equalising circuits
Split-parallel: parallel on ground for starting, split in flight
On failure in split, only the loads on that bus are lost; essential loads transfer to the healthy bus
In parallel, one fault can trip the whole bus unless bus-tie protection acts
Trade-off between load sharing efficiency and fault containment

bank.q: Fuel quantity measurement is called the hardest cockpit parameter. Analyse why, and evaluate the correction methods used.
outline: Tank moves, fuel sloshes, aircraft pitches and rolls
Capacitance probes measure fuel level but dielectric constant changes with fuel type and temperature
Density changes mean volume measured is not mass
Compensator probe and temperature correction; multiple probes averaged
Attitude and acceleration corrections; dipstick check as fallback
Compare with a simple float gauge and state why it is inadequate

bank.q: Evaluate the consequences of fitting a fuse or circuit breaker larger than the wire's derated rating, and explain the role of current limiters and limiting resistors.
outline: Wire becomes the fusible element; insulation chars and fire risk rises
Short circuit may not be cleared before damage
Current limiter: high rupturing capacity device for heavy feeder faults
Limiting resistor reduces fault current to a level a smaller breaker can clear
Coordination: device time-current curve must lie below the wire damage curve
Undersizing also fails: nuisance trips and load loss

glossary.def: Auxiliary power unit: a small gas turbine in the tail that supplies electrical and pneumatic power on the ground and in flight if needed.
Integrated drive generator: an engine-driven generator with a built-in constant-speed drive so it always produces 400 Hz AC.
A heavy-duty relay that makes and breaks a main power circuit under control of a switch or protection relay.
A contactor that joins two busbars, either to share load between generators or to let one generator feed both sides.
Circuit of diodes that converts alternating current into direct current.
The pressure produced by motion, equal to half the density times the square of the speed, written ½ρV².
The pressure of still air at the aircraft's altitude, sensed by ports on the fuselage side.
Junction of two unlike metals that produces a small voltage proportional to the temperature difference between its hot and cold ends.
Correction applied for the temperature of the thermocouple's reference end, so the reading is the hot-end temperature only.
The small DC current fed to a generator's field winding, which sets the strength of the magnetic field and hence the output voltage.
Supplying the field current; a generator with no excitation produces no output.
Automatically removing non-essential loads so a reduced power source can keep the essential ones running.
A busbar reserved for loads that must keep running: flight instruments, radios, flight controls, and minimum lighting.
Reducing a component's allowed current below its catalogue value to allow for high ambient temperature, altitude, or tightly bundled wires.
Resettable protection device that opens on overcurrent and can be reset by the crew after a fault is cleared.
Slow-acting protective device for heavy feeder circuits; carries normal current indefinitely but opens on a large sustained fault.
External cart or pit supply that feeds the aircraft busbars while the engines and APU are off.
High-intensity radiated fields: strong external radio or radar energy the aircraft's wiring must not pick up as a false signal.
Fuel tank sensor whose capacitance changes as fuel rises between its plates; used to infer fuel level.
Flashing red beacon that warns ground crew and other traffic that the aircraft is about to move or is running.
Forward-facing open tube on the fuselage that senses total pressure for the airspeed indicator.
Instrument that displays engine shaft speed, usually as a percentage of the maximum rated speed.
Transformer rectifier unit; steps AC down and rectifies it to DC, typically giving 28 V DC from 115 V AC.
Built-in test equipment: self-check circuits inside a unit that report faults to the cockpit or a maintenance panel.
